title: Mr. X & The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
text:
Decision
Mr. X & The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-162236-Q9X0T0
Published on 10 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Commission was justified, under sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act, in refusing access to records relating to its review of a merger involving two named private companies
10 July 2026
Background
In an FOI request dated 8 April 2025, the applicant sought access to records relating to the Commission’s review of a merger involving two named private companies. In particular, the request sought access to relevant submissions, requests from the Commission for further information and responses to same, and records of interviews carried out by the Commission. In the course of subsequent correspondence exchanged between the parties, the Commission advised the applicant that his request was likely to involve a voluminous amount of records, and sought to narrow the scope of the request. Thereafter, the applicant refined his request, specifically seeking access to i) any cover letters from participating third parties to include any indices or lists of attachments, ii) any legal reports and iii) any technical reports, relating to the Commission’s review of the merger identified in his original request.
In its decision on the FOI request dated 3 July 2025, the Commission refused the request, citing sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act as grounds for its refusal. On 28 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review from the Commission of its initial decision. In its internal review decision dated 18 August 2025, the Commission affirmed its original decision. On 24 October 2025, the applicant sought a review from this Office of the Commission’s decision on his FOI request.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the relevant correspondence exchanged between the parties, the submissions made by the applicant in his application for review and the submissions made by the Commission in support of its decision. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
This review is solely concerned with whether the Commission was justified, under sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act, in refusing to grant the applicant access to the records sought.
Preliminary Matters
Before I address the substantive issues arising, I wish to make some preliminary points. First of all, it is important to note that section 22(12)(b) of the FOI Act provides that a decision to refuse to grant a request shall be presumed not to have been justified unless the head of the relevant FOI body shows to the Information Commissioner's satisfaction that its decision was justified. This means that the onus is on the Commission of satisfying this Office that it was entitled to rely on the relevant provisions of the FOI Act in its decision on the applicant’s FOI request.
Secondly, section 25(3) of the FOI Act requires me to take all reasonable precautions in the course of a review to prevent disclosure of information contained in an exempt record. This means that the extent to which I can describe the contents of the record at issue is limited.
It is also relevant to note that the FOI Act places no constraints on the uses to which information released under FOI can subsequently be put. Accordingly, the release of information under FOI is generally regarded as release, at least potentially, to the world at large.
Finally, section 13(4) of the FOI Act requires that, subject to the legislation, any reasons a requester gives for making a request shall be disregarded. This means that this Office cannot have regard to the applicant’s motives for seeking the records in question, except insofar as those motives reflect what might be regarded as public interest factors in favour of release of information, where the FOI Act requires a consideration of public interest.
Analysis and Findings
The records at issue
The Commission identified a total of 275 relevant records, across nine categories. It cited section 35(1) of the FOI Act as a basis to withhold all 275 the records in full, due to the circumstances in which they were provided (i.e. by parties participating in the merger review process). In addition to relying on section 35(1) in respect of each of the records, the Commission applied the remainder of the exemptions on which it relied to withhold the records as follows:
1. Records 1 and 2 are Requests for Information (RFIs) issued by the Commission to the two primary parties involved in the merger during Phase 2 of the merger review process. The Commission relied on sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1) to withhold both records in full.
2. Records 3 to 59 are responses received by the Commission to the RFIs issued during Phase 2. The Commission relied on sections 36(1) and 37(1) to withhold all of these records in full.
3. Records 60 to 63 are third-party submissions made to the Commission during its Phase 2 investigation process in relation to the merger. The Commission withheld each of these records in full under sections 36(1) and 37(1).
4. Records 64 to 71 are third party submissions made to the Commission during its Phase 1
investigation process in relation to the merger. Again, the Commission withheld each of these records in full under sections 36(1) and 37(1).
5. Record 72 is the Commission’s Phase 2 report on the merger, which it withheld from release in full under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1).
6. Records 73 to 90 are notes of interviews conducted by the Commission with third parties in relation to the merger, all of which the Commission again withheld in full under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1).
7. Records 91 and 92 are further RFIs issued by the Commission in May 2024 to the two primary parties involved in the merger. Again, the Commission cited sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1) to fully withhold these two records.
8. Records 93 to 141 comprise the response to the May 2024 RFI from one of the principal parties to merger. The Commission relied on the following provisions of the FOI Act to fully withhold each of these records –
o records 93, 101 to 103, 115, 118, 132 and 139 were withheld under section 36(1);
o records 94, 98 to 100, 112, 114, 116 to 117, 119 to 131, 133 to 138 and 141 were withheld under sections 36(1) and 37(1);
o record 106 was withheld under sections 29(1), 30(1) and 36(1).
9. Records 142 to 275 comprise the response to the May 2024 RFI from the other principal party to the merger. The Commission relied on the following provisions of the FOI Act to withhold each of these records in full –
o records 142 and 150 were withheld under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1);
o records 143 to 145, 152, 155, 160 to 167, 169 to 171, 173 to 174, 181, 183 to 184, 187 to 188, 191 to 194, 196 to 198, 201, 207, 209, 212 to 214, 216, 218 to 219, 221 to 227, 229 to 230, 239, 242 to 244, 247 to 255, 258 to 263, 268 and 270 were withheld under sections 36(1) and 37(1);
o records 147 to 149, 151, 153 to 154, 156 to 159, 176 to 180, 182, 185 to 186, 189 to 190, 195, 199 to 200, 202 to 206, 208, 210 to 211, 215, 217, 220, 228, 231, 233 to 234, 236 to 238, 245 to 246, 256 to 257, 264 to 267, 269 and 271 to 275 were withheld under sections and 36(1);
o records 168, 232, 235 and 240 to 241 were withheld under section 37(1).
Section 35(1)
In circumstances where the Commission relied on section 35(1) to withhold in full all of the records at issue, I consider it appropriate to examine the applicability of this provision of the FOI Act first of all. In its submissions, the Commission relied primarily on subsection (a) of section 35(1), while also noting its view that subsection (b) was also applicable. In the circumstances, I consider section 35(1)(a) the most appropriate provision of the FOI Act under which to examine the Commission’s arguments that the records are exempt from release.
Section 35(1)(a) provides for the mandatory refusal of a request where the record sought contains information given to an FOI body in confidence. This provision of the FOI Act contains four requirements, all of which must be satisfied in order for a record to fall within its scope;
• the information must have been given to an FOI body in confidence;
• the information must have been given on the understanding that it would be treated by the FOI body as confidential;
• disclosure of the information would be likely to prejudice the giving to the body of further similar information from the same person or other persons; and
• it is important to the body that such further similar information should continue to be given to the body.
The Commission’s submissions
Section 35(1)(a)
In its submissions, the Commission noted that a key component in evaluating the applicability of section 35(1)(a) is an assessment of the circumstances in which the relevant information was provided and the expectation of confidentiality. It argued that, in this case, the circumstances in which the information in the records was imparted to it, and the expectations of confidentiality on the part of the parties providing the information, clearly engaged section 35(1)(a). The Commission argued that the information in the records had been provided explicitly and implicitly on a confidential basis, in circumstances where there was a clear and mutual understanding that it would be treated as such. It stated that the nature of merger reviews, as set out in its guidance and procedures, requires undertakings to provide full details of a proposed transaction in order to enable a proper assessment to be carried out. According to the Commissions, this necessarily involves the disclosure of information that would not otherwise enter the public domain.
In relation to the four requirements of section 35(1)(a), the Commission submitted that, in the context of merger reviews, all four are clearly met. It stated that its merger review process requires notifying parties to provide comprehensive and highly sensitive information regarding their businesses, including detailed financial and commercial data, forward-looking business strategies, and internal assessments of markets and competitors. It noted that confidential submissions from relevant third parties are also sought during this process. It argued that such information is provided explicitly and implicitly on a confidential basis, in circumstances where there is a clear and mutual understanding that it will be treated as such.
The first and second requirements
The Commission argued that the information at issue was provided to it in the context of a formal merger review process and for the limited purpose of enabling the assessment of the proposed transaction. In such circumstances, according to the Commission, it was reasonable for the relevant parties, including the notifying parties, customers and competitors, to expect that such information would be treated as confidential and not disclosed more widely. The Commission stated that this element of confidentiality underpins the merger review process and it would not be possible for it to perform this function without it. In these circumstances, it argued that the first and second requirements of section 35(1)(a) are satisfied.
The third requirement
The Commission argued that the third requirement is also met, in circumstances where (according to its submissions) disclosure of the records would be likely to prejudice its receipt of further similar information. It argued that if the parties involved in a merger or other related third parties could not rely on the confidentiality of their submissions, they may limit the scope or detail of the information provided, decline to provide commercially sensitive material or be unwilling to engage with it as part of the merger review process. According to the Commission, disclosure of the records at issue would expose, or allow competitors to derive, sensitive commercial information relating to the parties involved, which would in turn undermine the willingness of future parties to provide it with full and candid information. The Commission argued that such an outcome would prejudice the provision of further similar information to it and would have a direct and detrimental impact on its ability to carry out effective merger reviews, which it argued by extension would have a detrimental impact on businesses and consumers.
The fourth requirement
The Commission argued that the fourth requirement in section 35(1)(a) is fundamental in the context of the records under review. It stated that the merger review process is heavily dependent on the voluntary provision of complete, accurate and candid information by notifying parties and third parties, including highly sensitive commercial matters. It stated that the disclosure of sensitive commercial information in the records at issue would deter parties from engaging with it in future. The Commission argued that it is of the utmost importance to it that it continues to be provided with such information on a confidential basis and argued that, without this, it would be unable to properly assess the competitive effects of mergers or to fulfil its statutory mandate. The Commission argued that the importance of confidentiality in this process cannot be overstated, and that such confidentiality underpins the quality and reliability of evidence available to it, as well as the willingness of stakeholders to cooperate and the overall integrity and effectiveness of the merger review process.
The public interest test – section 35(3)
The exemption at section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act is subject to a public interest test in section 35(3), which provides that subsection (a) of section 35(1) shall not apply in relation to a case in which, in the opinion of the FOI body, the public interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the FOI request.
In its submissions on section 35(3), the Commission stated that the balance of the public interest in this case weighs clearly in favour of refusal. It stated that, although there is a recognised public interest in transparency and accountability, this must be balanced against the strong public interest in ensuring the effective enforcement of competition law, maintaining a robust and credible merger review process and protecting the flow of confidential information necessary for regulatory decision-making. The Commission noted the decision of the Supreme Court in Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources v The Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57 (“the eNet case”), in which the Court stated that the public interest in favour of disclosure cannot be equated with the general public interest in openness and transparency set out in the FOI Act. Instead, the Court found that the public interest in disclosure must be something more than the general public interest in disclosure and there must be a “sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason” in order “to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”. The Commission argued that, in the present case, there is no such reason that would tip the balance in favour of releasing the records. Rather, it argued, disclosure of the records would undermine confidence in the confidentiality of the merger review process and could significantly impair its ability to obtain the information required to carry out its functions effectively, which it stated would be contrary to the public interest.
In addition, the Commission made submissions in the context of the public interest test provided for in certain other exemptions in the FOI Act upon which it relied, and I consider it appropriate to include these in an examindation of the public interest test in section 35(3). In particular, it noted that transparency regarding the merger review process is ensured through the publication of Merger Determinations on its website, which it said set out its conclusions and reasoning in respect to mergers. The Commission argued that this ensures an appropriate level of accountability without disclosing material that could prejudice its functions.
The applicant’s submissions
Section 35(1)(a)
In his submissions on section 35(1)(a), the applicant first of all argued that the Commission had erred in withholding the records in full, and that partial release should have been possible, given that a number of records appear to have been created by Commission employees. The applicant argued that section 35(2) of the FOI Act (which provides for the disapplication of section 35(1) in certain circumstances, which I examine further below) should apply to such records.
The applicant argued that the statutory function of the Commission is to promote compliance with, and enforce, competition and consumer protection law in Ireland. He stated that this is distinct from a purely commercial impetus and carries with it, by definition, a higher degree of accountability to the public at large. The applicant argued that this Office should take into account the inherent organisational purpose of the Commission when making its determination.
The public interest test – section 35(3)
In relation to section 35(3), the applicant noted that section 11(3) of the FOI Act requires FOI bodies to have a general regard to the need to achieve greater openness in their activities and to strengthen their accountability and improve the quality of their decision-making. He stated that his purpose in making his FOI request was to understand the reason that an FOI body came to a particular decision, and argued that it followed that the public interest would be better served by the release, rather than the withholding, of the records.
My analysis
Section 35(2)
In circumstances where the applicant argued that section 35(2) is potentially applicable to some of the records, and where (if it applies) section 35(2) would preclude the Commission’s reliance on 35(1) in respect of those records, I take the view that it is appropriate to examine the former provision of the FOI Act first of all. Section 35(2) provides that section 35(1) as a whole shall not apply to a record which was:
(i) prepared by a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body or a service provider;
(ii) prepared in the course of the performance of his or her functions;
(iii) UNLESS disclosure would constitute a breach of a duty of confidence which is owed to a person other than an FOI body, a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body, or a service provider to, an FOI body.
As noted above, the applicant suggested that section 35(2) is potentially engaged in circumstances where certain of the records were prepared by employees of the Commission. I accept that this is the case in respect of the relevant records, and would also note that it seems to be straightforwardly the case the records were prepared by such staff members in the performance of their functions. Thus, I accept that the first two conditions in section 35(2) are met in respect of the relevant records. I make this finding in respect of records 1, 2, and 72 to 92 (in other words all records that were created by staff of the Commission).
The remaining question that I must consider is whether the release of these records would constitute a breach of a duty of confidence that is provided for by an agreement or statute or otherwise by law and is owed by the Commission to a person other than an FOI body or its staff. It is well settled that a duty of confidence provided otherwise by law includes an equitable duty of confidence.
In the Supreme Court decision in the case of Mahon v Post Publications Ltd [2007] 3 I.R. 338 (“the Mahon case”) Fennelly J confirmed that the requirements for a successful action based on a breach of an equitable duty of confidence, at least in a commercial setting, are found in the judgment of Megarry J in Coco v. A. N. Clark (Engineers) Ltd. [1969] R.P.C. 41, at 47:
“[T]hree elements are normally required if, apart from contract, a case of breach ofconfidence is to succeed. First, the information itself ... must 'have the necessaryquality of confidence about it'. Secondly, that information must have been imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence.Thirdly, there must be anunauthorised use of that information to the detriment of the party communicating it."
Fennelly J summarised or restated the requirements of what he called “the contours”
of the equitable doctrine of confidence as follows:
“1. the information must in fact be confidential or secret: it must ... “have the necessary quality of confidence about it”;
2. it must have been communicated by the possessor of the information in circumstances which impose an obligation of confidence or trust on the person receiving it;
3. it must be wrongfully communicated by the person receiving it or by another person who is aware of the obligation of confidence.”
In previous decisions, this Office has stated its understanding that "detriment" could arise simply where the relevant information is disclosed without the consent of the party to whom the information relates.
In the section of its submissions addressing section 35(1)(b) (which relates to the question of the existence of a duty of confidence, and which contains essentially the same test as that set out in section 35(2)), the Commission argued that such a duty exists in this case, and that to release the records would constitute a breach of this duty. It argued that this is the case in circumstances where, in the context of merger reviews, obligations of confidentiality arise both explicitly (through processes and communications) and implicitly, given the sensitive nature of the information provided. It noted that, for the purposes of section 35, the circumstances in which information is provided is of critical importance, and stated that this is particularly relevant in the context of merger reviews. The Commission argued that parties participating in the merger review process must be assured that the information they provide, which is often commercially sensitive in nature, will be treated with the utmost confidentiality. The Commission stated that any perception that such information could be disclosed, including via FOI requests, would fundamentally undermine that assurance and, in turn the willingness of the relevant parties to engage fully with it.
I have examined the records outlined above which were created by staff of the Commission in the performance of their functions. In my view, the records comprising RFIs (in other words records 1, 2, 91 and 92) contain significant amounts of detail regarding the commercial operations of the parties to the merger. In particular, I note that the RFIs refer back to previous information provided to the Commission by the parties, and that this information goes into quite granular detail regarding certain previous agreements signed by the parties. Furthermore, I take the view that record 72 (the Commission’s Phase 2 report on the merger) contains significant and substantial details in relation to the commercial operations of both parties to the merger. Moreover, I consider that the records comprising interviews carried out by the Commission with relevant third parties (records 73 to 90) contain information provided by the third parties relating to their operations and commercial activities. I take the view that the parties to whom this information relates, and who in large part provided the information to the Commission, are entitled to regard the information as having provided in confidence, and that they have a reasonable expectation that the Commission would treat it as confidential. I make this finding where the material in the records that relates to the third parties is, to my mind, information about the commercial workings of the parties, and is in all likelihood commercially sensitive information. I am satisfied that the three-pronged test for the existence of an equitable duty of confidence, as set out by Fennelly J in the Mahon case, is satisfied in respect of this information.
Accordingly, my view is that an equitable duty of confidence exists in respect of the information in these records, and that this duty is owed by the Commission to the relevant third-party commercial entities. In other words, the duty of confidence is owed to parties other than an FOI body, a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body, or a service provider to, an FOI body. Thus, the third requirement for the operation of section 35(2) is not met. I therefore find that section 35(2) of the FOI Act does not operate in this case to preclude the Commission’s reliance on section 35(1).
Section 35(1)(a)
It remains for me to examine whether the records are, in fact, exempt from release under section 35(1)(a).
In relation to the first two requirements of section 35(1)(a), I accept that the information in the records was given to the Commission in confidence and on the understanding that it would be treated as confidential. I am satisfied that this is the case in respect of both the information in the records created by the Commission that pertains to relevant third-party commercial entities, and the information in the remainder of the records that was provided by those entities to the Commission. I make this finding in circumstances where I accept the arguments of the Commission to the effect that both the parties to the merger, and the relevant third parties, have provided (in the context of the merger review process) information which is sensitive regarding their operations, finances and strategies, and their assessments of markets and competitors. I also accept that this information which is not in the public domain. My view is that the Commission’s arguments regarding the first two requirements of section 35(1)(a) effectively state its position that the merger review process is known to the parties involved, and that the information necessary for the Commission to carry out the review can reasonably be regarded by the parties providing it as being confidential information. Essentially, it seems to me that the review process is bought into by the parties engaging with the Commission on the understanding of the confidentiality of the information provided.
I am also satisfied that the third requirement of section 35(1)(a) is met in this case. I am quite prepared to accept that the release of the information in the records that pertains to the commercial operations and inner workings of both the parties to the merger and the third-party entities would be likely to prejudice the giving to it of further similar information. It should be noted in this regard that I am not required to satisfy myself that the disclosure of the information in the records would definitely prejudice the supply of the relevant information, and it is sufficient that disclosure would be likely to prejudice such supply. I am satisfied that this standard is met in this case. In particular, I accept the arguments of the Commission that the release of the records at issue might reasonably be expected to undermine the willingness of future parties to provide it with full and candid information, and that such an outcome might have a direct and detrimental impact on its ability to carry out effective merger reviews. It should be noted that “prejudice” in this context need not mean that, for example, the provision of similar information in future might not occur at all or that the information-gathering process carried out by the Commission in the course of carrying out merger reviews is defeated entirely; it is sufficient that, for example, the quality or timeliness of the information provided might be expected to be adversely impacted. Based on the contents of the records and the arguments of the Commission, I accept that such an expectation is reasonable.
Finally in relation to section 35(1)(a), I accept that the fourth requirement is also met. It seems to me to be self-evident that the type of information at issue is of central importance to the Commission in terms of its ability to effectively carry out merger reviews. Indeed, it is difficult to see how the Commission could perform this function to any meaningful degree should the information it requires for the purpose not be forthcoming for any reason.
Accordingly, on the basis of the analysis above, my view is that each of the four requirements in section 35(1)(a) are met in this case. In particular, I accept the Commission’s arguments that the circumstances in which the information in the records was imparted to it (by the parties to the merger as well as relevant third-party entities) entail a clear mutual expectation of confidentiality. I therefore find that the records at issue are within the scope of the exemption provided for in section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act.
Section 35(3)
It remains for me to examine whether the public interest would on balance be better served by the granting rather than the withholding of the information in the records, under section 35(3) of the FOI Act.
On the one hand, section 35 itself recognises a public interest in protecting confidentiality. In this case, I accept that there is a public interest in protecting the confidentiality of these particular records, which serves the flow of information from the parties involved in the merger, and other relevant third-party commercial entities, to the Commission. On the other hand, I must consider whether there is a public interest in disclosing the specific content of these records.
In carrying out any review, this Office has regard to the general principles of openness and transparency set out in section 11(3) of the FOI Act, which were highlighted by the applicant in his submissions. As the applicant noted, section 11(3) provides that an FOI body must have regard to the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. However, it is equally the case that, as flagged by the Commission in its submissions, the Supreme Court in the eNet case has found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and that “there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”.
In the applicant’s submissions, he stated that the reason for his FOI request was to try and understand the reasons why the Commission had taken its decision on the merger. I accept that this a valid argument for the purposes of section 35(3). There certainly exists, to my mind, a very valid public interest in knowing how the Commission reaches decisions on merger reviews.
This being said, it should also be noted that the purpose of the FOI Act is not to open up to scrutiny the commercial workings of private entities. While I am quite prepared to accept that a public interest certainly exists in casting greater light on the operations and decision-making processes of the Commission, I do not take the view that this public interest requires the opening up to scrutiny of the commercial and financial details of the parties to the merger and of the relevant third-party commercial entities. Moreover, my view is that the public interest in knowing the reasons for the Commission’s decision is linked to an equally valid public interest in the protection of the consumer (against, for example, the development of monopolies in certain sectors). However, again my view is that this public interest does not entitle the world at large to access information that goes to the inner workings of private companies.
It is relevant, in the context of the public interest I have identified in understanding the reasons for the Commission’s decisions, that – as noted above – the Commission publishes Merger Determinations on its website. These determinations are, to my mind, comprehensive and thorough (for example, the relevant determination report on the Commission website regarding the merger at issue in this case runs to some 260 pages and contain a significant level of detail in relation to the Commission’s investigation, reasoning and findings). My view is that, in publishing detailed Merger Determinations on its website, the Commission is clearly attempting to ensure an appropriate level of transparency regarding its own operations, while at the same time protecting commercially sensitive information relating to private enterprises. I consider that the public interest identified by the applicant is to a large degree met by the Commission’s publication of Merger Determinations.
Accordingly, my finding is that, for the purposes of section 35(3) of the FOI Act, the balance of the public interest favours the withholding, rather than the release, of the records at issue.
My findings
Based on my analysis above, I find that the Commission was justified under section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act in withholding access in full to the records at issue. In those circumstances, I am not required to examine the extent to which the records might also be exempt from release under the other provisions of the FOI Act upon which the Commission relied.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the decision of the Commission. I find that it was justified under section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act in refusing access to the records sought.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.

Neill Dougan
Investigator
respondent: The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
